title_en: Mexico and China agree to create working group to boost trade
content_en:
Economy chief Marcelo ‌Ebrard has called ‌for steps to narrow the gap needed for Mexico ‌to export agricultural and food products to China.
Mexico’s Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China on Thursday. Photo: AFP
Mexico and China agreed on Monday to create a working group focused on bilateral economic priorities, Mexico’s ⁠Economy Ministry said.
Economy ministers Marcelo ‌Ebrard of Mexico and Wang Wentao of China will look at ways to boost Mexican exports to China, the ministry said.
During talks in Beijing, Ebrard ⁠highlighted a persistent trade imbalance, noting that China ‌is set to export more than US$130 billion in goods to Mexico ‌this year, compared with roughly US$10 billion ⁠in ⁠Mexican shipments to China, the ministry said.
He called ‌for steps to narrow the gap, urging Beijing to expedite ‌sanitary ‌protocols - some stalled for a decade - needed for Mexico ‌to export agricultural and food products, ⁠including beef, pork, avocados, limes, sorghum and processed ⁠seafood.
The high-level meeting followed talks last week between Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and ‌Chinese President ‌Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in southern China.
By Reuters

title_en: UK sanctions Myanmar president, military figures after genocide ruling
content_en:
The UN’s International Court of Justice last ‌week ‌ruled that ‌Myanmar committed ⁠genocide against the ⁠Muslim Rohingya minority in ‌2017.
Rohingya refugees attend a mass gathering during a visit by Bangladesh Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman at a refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh on Friday. Photo: EPA
Britain ⁠on Monday announced sanctions against five ‌people under its Myanmar and global human rights sanctions ⁠regimes, including senior ‌members of the nation’s military.
The ‌sanctions were announced ⁠after ⁠the ‌International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled last ‌week ‌ruled that ‌Myanmar committed state-sponsored ⁠genocide against the ⁠Muslim Rohingya minority population in ‌2017.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said restrictions would be placed on Min Aung Hlaing, and four other senior military members from the country in South Asia.
Miliband also said new legislation will be passed to stop the supply of aviation fuel to the country, which was known as Burma until 1989.
Last week he expelled Myanmar’s defence attache after the UN’s top court had ruled the country had committed genocide during a brutal 2017 military campaign.
Miliband told members of parliament on Monday the UK would raise the issue at the UN Security Council this week and there would be a dedicated meeting in two weeks’ time.
Speaking in the House of Commons, Miliband said: “On Thursday, we ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s defence attache, because we will not tolerate a serving representative of Myanmar’s military remaining imposed on UK soil.
“I can announce today that we have also imposed sanctions against four major generals and a brigadier general, senior military figures who oversaw troops that carried out egregious civilian killings and repression of the population across Myanmar.
“We know also that the Myanmar military has systematically used lethal air power against its own people. I do not believe the British people want any UK companies to have any links to such practices.
“So we will also introduce new legislation in the coming months to stop the export and supply of aviation fuel to Myanmar, which is used in such horrendous attacks.”
Britain’s Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs Secretary Ed Miliband and EU ambassador Caroline Wilson at the EU-UK summit in Brussels, Belgium on Friday. Photo: Reuters
Miliband also announced £3 million (US$3.87 million) to help Rohingya survivors, and a further £5 million of humanitarian help to support 350,000 Rohingya and Rakhine people.
He said those affected were struggling to access clean water and were suffering from malnourishment.
As well as the UK, 13 other countries on Monday “acknowledged” the ruling by the ICJ, the UN’s highest court.
The foreign ministers of Australia, Belgium, Canada, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Estonia, Iceland, Latvia, Luxembourg, New Zealand, Portugal, Spain, Gambia and Britain said Myanmar had “violated its obligations under the Genocide Convention”.
“We underscore that the Court’s judgment is binding upon Myanmar and call on Myanmar to comply fully with its obligations under international law, including the Court’s decision,” they said in a joint statement.
In the ruling last week, the ICJ found about 10,000 Rohingya were murdered during the clearance operation in the western Rakhine state that borders Bangladesh and the Bay of Bengal.
Reports included that entire villages were burnt down, and that women and girls were raped.
Miliband said more than 1.2 million refugees fled and were being supported by Bangladesh.
Myanmar’s leader during the genocide, Aung San Suu Kyi, who studied in England, was deposed by Myanmar’s military in 2021.
Myanmar's deposed leader Aung San Suu Kyi (left) in 2019 and Myanmar military chief Senior General Min Aung Hlaing in 2018. Photo: AFP
MPs heard that air strikes and violence from the Arakan Army were still happening.
“For this government, and I would argue for the whole international community, our response to a crime as profoundly shocking as genocide must reflect our values and must be matched by clear action,” Miliband said.
“We should also act cognisant of the fact that the appalling targeting of civilians by the Myanmar regime continues to this day, as does the discrimination and persecution of Rohingya and other communities.”
Miliband called for an “immediate pause in hostilities to enable humanitarian aid to get through, a stop to air strikes on civilians, and the release of political prisoners, as well as dialogue towards an inclusive political settlement”.
“Myanmar must stop ongoing violations, investigate, prosecute and punish perpetrators, and prevent such an atrocity from ever happening again,” he said.
“In the weeks and months ahead, I promise the House the UK will do everything we can to reinvigorate the political and diplomatic efforts to secure a just and lasting end to this appalling conflict.”
Reporting by Reuters, Agence France-Presse, dpa
By Agencies

title_en: Armenian PM unveils draft constitution, key to Azerbaijan peace deal
content_en:
Nikol Pashinyan proposed a constitution dropping Karabakh claims in a bid for peace with Baku, vowing to stand down if the text is rejected.
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan (centre) at his Armenia Ruling Civil Contract party headquarters in June. Photo: AP
Armenian leader Nikol Pashinyan unveiled a proposed new constitution on Monday that would get rid of a claim to the Karabakh region, saying it was the only way to reach a peace deal with Azerbaijan.
The Caucasus foes spent three decades locked in a territorial conflict over the mountainous region following the fall of the Soviet Union.
In a 2023 offensive, Baku retook the Armenian-populated region, forcing a mass exodus.
It has since demanded Yerevan remove claims to Karabakh from its constitution if it wants to finalise a peace treaty.
In an address to Armenians, Pashinyan promised to finalise a peace treaty with Azerbaijan should his countrymen back the new constitution in a referendum.
He vowed to stand down if the text was rejected.
Pashinyan said the new text rejects “the logic of conflict” and said the aim of the new constitution was to “ensure peace”.
The draft deletes the preamble from 1990, which included a clause for reunification with the Nagorno-Karabakh region and called for the international recognition of the genocide of Armenians by the Ottoman Empire.
US President Donald Trump (centre) with Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev (left) and Pashinyan at the White House in Washington in August last year. Photo: Reuters
The Armenian leader also said on Monday that practical work was starting on a new road – backed by US President Donald Trump – across southern Armenia linking Azerbaijan to its Nakhchivan exclave.
The project was a core part of progress towards a peace deal, which Trump is agitating for.
Armenia’s opposition has accused Pashinyan of bowing to Azerbaijan’s demands under pressure.
It has dubbed the new text “Aliyev’s Constitution” – after Azerbaijani leader Ilham Aliyev.
But Pashinyan told Armenians not to believe “that we are doing this for someone else under external pressure”.
Pashinyan – whose party is several seats short of a constitutional majority in parliament – called on the opposition not to block the referendum.
“If the people will vote against the constitution, I will resign,” he said.
Armenians call the region Artsakh and view it as their ancestral home, part of the ancient kingdom of Armenia that was populated by their ancestors 2,000 years ago.
Azerbaijan traces the history of its Muslim and Turkic tribes in the region to the Middle Ages.
The region was made part of Azerbaijan in Soviet times and following the Soviet collapse, it has been internationally recognised as part of Azerbaijan.
By Agence France-Presse
Sections: News / World / Europe / United States & Canada / Russia & Central Asia | Topics: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Diplomacy, War and conflict, Donald Trump, Central Asia, Ilham Aliyev, United States

title_en: UK’s former prince Andrew took ‘bribe’ to help Turkish heiress, UK court told
content_en:
Nebahat Isbilen, the wife of a jailed ex-Turkish MP, told London’s High Court she paid Andrew nearly US$1M to help her obtain UK residency.
Britain’s Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, formerly Prince Andrew. Photo: AP
Britain’s former prince Andrew received £750,000 (US$976,000) as an alleged “bribe” to help a Turkish heiress, the High Court in London was told on Monday, with the disgraced British royal due to testify in the civil trial.
The claim around the payment emerged at the start of the anticipated four-month trial, which pits Nebahat Isbilen, whose family founded the Evyap soap and cosmetics group, against her former adviser and businessman, Selman Turk.
Isbilen, the wife of a jailed Turkish former MP, is suing Turk, alleging he misappropriated tens of millions of pounds of her funds and did not explain where the money went, which he denies.
Andrew, now known as Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor and who is not accused of wrongdoing, returned the £750,000 after Isbilen wrote to him at the start of the legal proceedings several years ago, according to her legal submissions.
However, he is expected to give evidence on December 14, after the judge hearing the case earlier this year permitted Turk to issue him with a witness summons, compelling him to appear at the trial.
The former prince is the first member of Britain’s royal family since 1870 to receive a summons requiring him to give High Court evidence, according to The Times.
It is the latest humiliation for King Charles’ younger brother, who was last year stripped of his royal titles following revelations stemming from his friendship with the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The legal battle between Isbilen, 81, and Turk has been waged in Britain’s courts for several years and has spotlighted the involvement of Andrew and his ex-wife, Sarah Ferguson, in various financial dealings connected to the case.
[embedded media]
Isbilen’s legal filings claim Turk sent about £2 million to a company called Alphabet Capital, some of which was transferred to Andrew and his ex-wife.
Isbilen has claimed she turned to Turk for help to get her fortune out of Turkey after her husband was jailed in 2015 on what he says were politically motivated charges.
She alleges Turk “lied to her” about the purpose of the £750,000 payment to Andrew.
But Turk’s lawyer, Joshua Hitchens, wrote in legal submissions unveiled on Monday that “her own case is that she understood that the payment to the Duke of York was a bribe, either for assistance with her passport or her UK residency”.
Hitchens goes on to claim the payment was really about discussing “her husband’s case” with Andrew, detailing a December 2019 dinner at Turk’s London flat requested by Isbilen and attended by the former Duke and Duchess of York.
“She cannot have believed that the £750,000 was a disguised fee for help with a passport, or with a visa,” Hitchens stated.
“The payment was what Mr Turk told the bank it was: a gift, made in the hope of Mr Mountbatten-Windsor taking steps to assist her husband.”
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Burnham to ignore ‘stuck in the past’ ex-PMs as he hails UK’s EU reset
content_en:
Former Conservative leaders including Rishi Sunak, Theresa May, David Cameron, and Boris Johnson warned against reopening Brexit divisions.
Britain’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham at parliament in Westminster, London on Monday. Photo: PRU / AFP
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham accused predecessors who have warned him against reigniting the Brexit debate of being “stuck in the past” on Monday, as he trumpeted his EU reset deal.
Burnham has in recent weeks smashed a general consensus that Britain’s acrimonious departure from the European Union was done and dusted, floating the possibility that Britain could apply to rejoin.
The comments have seen pro-Brexit voices from the 2016 EU referendum reorganise to prepare for probable looming battles over Britain’s long-term relationship with the bloc.
In recent days, former Conservative prime ministers Rishi Sunak, Theresa May, David Cameron and Boris Johnson have all urged Labour leader Burnham not to reopen old wounds.
“I’m not sure they’re the people I’ll be listening to here because they left Britain with a bad Brexit deal,” Burnham told broadcasters.
“They’re stuck in the past because they can’t face up to the bad deal that they did.”
In Brussels on Friday, Burnham and the EU’s top officials sealed agreements to ease trade and youth mobility, although they kicked down the road tricky disagreements over British university fees for EU students.
The UK government argues the deals will eventually add £17 billion (US$22 billion) to Britain’s economy per annum, easing cost-of-living pressures and providing opportunities for young people.
Former British prime minister Rishi Sunak. Photo: AP
“I want to lead Britain forward to a more hopeful future, get the economy growing again, get cost of living down for people, lower energy bills,” Burnham said.
“All of these things can be achieved by a more positive, constructive relationship with the European Union.
“I believe it will be better for Britain to take this path and I won’t be listening to those voices who put us here in the first place,” he added.
Sunak, premier from 2022 to 2024, told Sky News that restarting the “divisive” Brexit debate would become an “all-consuming” distraction for Burnham’s government.
In an interview with the BBC, May – whose 2016 to 2019 tenure was dominated by her failure to pass a Brexit deal – urged Burnham to “accept Brexit and move on”.
It echoed warnings from Cameron, who called the referendum and resigned following the result, and Johnson, who took Britain out of the bloc in early 2020.
The comments evoked the so-called Brexit wars that dominated political discourse for years following the narrow vote.
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch at the annual conference of the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) in London, Britain on Monday. Photo: EPA
On Monday, Nigel Farage, the leader of the anti-EU Reform UK party, was expected to say that “going backwards into the EU’s orbit would be a disaster for the very British businesses that are trying to compete and innovate”, according to excerpts released by his office.
Meanwhile, Conservative opposition leader Kemi Badenoch said rejoining the EU “is not going to fix” Britain’s stagnant economy.
Burnham’s office said he would tell parliament in an afternoon speech that Friday’s agreements mean there is a “very real prospect that the next decade can be a much better one for Britain than the one we have just lived through”.
Burnham intends to discuss with Brussels options for future ties with the EU over the next 12 months. He has said the British public will be “the boss” over the future relationship, but has not said whether this means another referendum.
He has ruled out free movement or rejoining the single market or customs union during this parliament, which will end when he calls a general election, expected in 2029.
Several Labour MPs have praised Burnham for breaking the taboo over Brexit and have said he should put rejoining in the party’s next manifesto, but the party is divided.
By Agence France-Presse

It echoed warnings from Cameron, who called the referendum and resigned following the result, and Johnson, who took Britain out of the bloc in early 2020.
The comments evoked the so-called Brexit wars that dominated political discourse for years following the narrow vote.
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch at the annual conference of the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) in London, Britain on Monday. Photo: EPA
On Monday, Nigel Farage, the leader of the anti-EU Reform UK party, was expected to say that “going backwards into the EU’s orbit would be a disaster for the very British businesses that are trying to compete and innovate”, according to excerpts released by his office.
Meanwhile, Conservative opposition leader Kemi Badenoch said rejoining the EU “is not going to fix” Britain’s stagnant economy.
Burnham’s office said he would tell parliament in an afternoon speech that Friday’s agreements mean there is a “very real prospect that the next decade can be a much better one for Britain than the one we have just lived through”.
Burnham intends to discuss with Brussels options for future ties with the EU over the next 12 months. He has said the British public will be “the boss” over the future relationship, but has not said whether this means another referendum.
He has ruled out free movement or rejoining the single market or customs union during this parliament, which will end when he calls a general election, expected in 2029.
Several Labour MPs have praised Burnham for breaking the taboo over Brexit and have said he should put rejoining in the party’s next manifesto, but the party is divided.

title_en: UK Grand Theft Auto VI hacker gets 7-year sentence
content_en:
Arion Kurtaj, 21, walked free from a London court on time served after pleading guilty to the 2021–2022 Rockstar Games hacks.
Grand Theft Auto VI was released last week. Photo: Reuters
A UK court sentenced a British hacker to seven years in prison on Monday for a series of cyberattacks, including leaking footage from Grand Theft Auto VI years before the blockbuster game’s release.
Having already served years in custody, Arion Kurtaj, aged 21, was entitled to walk free immediately, Judge Mark Turner said at London’s Woolwich Crown Court.
Kurtaj, who is autistic, pleaded guilty last week to hacking major companies between 2021 and 2022, including Grand Theft Auto-maker Rockstar Games, mobile operator BT/EE, digital bank Revolut and ride-hailing giant Uber.
Turner described the offences as “sophisticated attacks upon big companies”.
“Don’t let this happen again,” he added.
The judge said his sentencing decision required “balancing the seriousness of what you did with, on the other hand, your young age” and medical diagnoses.
[embedded media]
Kurtaj was a teenager when he carried out the attacks as a key member of the so-called Lapsus$ hacking group.
He was initially charged over hacking BT/EE and placed in a hotel for his own protection from rival hackers in September 2022, according to the Crown Prosecution Service.
But from his hotel room, he went on to carry out cyberattacks on Revolut, Uber and Rockstar.
Using just a mobile phone, the hotel’s wifi-connected television and an Amazon Fire TV Stick, he broke into Rockstar systems and obtained 90 videos of the highly anticipated GTA VI game.
He leaked the videos online under the username “TeaPotUberHacker”, more than a year before the first official footage was released by Rockstar, causing a frenzy across the video game industry.
The hack disrupted the release strategy for the sixth instalment of the Grand Theft Auto franchise, which was finally released last week after a 13-year wait.
In 2023, a jury concluded that Kurtaj, whom psychiatrists at the time had deemed unfit to stand trial, was responsible for numerous computer misuse, fraud and blackmail offences.
Due to the severity of his autism, he was placed under a hospital order where he remained for two years before being found fit to stand trial, his lawyers said.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Nato vows space defence after Russia nuclear satellite report
content_en:
German media reported that Moscow is planning a launch within weeks that would give it the ability to destroy satellites.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz (right) and Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte at the Chancellery in Berlin, Germany on Monday. Photo: EPA
Nato chief Mark Rutte said on Monday the alliance would defend against threats in space when asked about German media reports that Russia may be preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.
The media reports, citing unnamed German military and BND spy agency sources, said Moscow was thought to be planning such a launch in the coming weeks, giving it the capability to destroy other satellites.
Rutte, asked about the reports while visiting Berlin, vowed: “We will always make sure that we defend every inch of Nato territory and that includes making sure that we are safe when it comes to the space element.”
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, speaking alongside Rutte, did not confirm or deny the media reports but voiced concern.
“Reports that Russia is planning to introduce nuclear weaponry into space are not new, yet they remain no less shocking,” he said.
“They reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue,” added Merz, whose chancellery oversees the BND foreign intelligence agency.
A German government spokesman earlier said that the reports were being taken “very seriously,” though he did not confirm them either and warned against causing “excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers”.
[embedded media]
Public broadcasters WDR and NDR, along with the Sueddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, reported that Russia planned to launch a satellite dubbed “Sputnik-S” equipped with a nuclear warhead some time in the coming weeks.
The outlets, citing unnamed sources, said the intelligence reports about the plans had recently been shared among several Nato countries and that the German government had been briefed on the matter.
The satellite had been stored in the Moscow region, according to the news outlets, and could be used to disrupt or destroy important communications and observation satellites orbiting Earth.
The BND declined to comment when questioned by Agence France-Presse, while the German military’s space command pointed to general remarks from Defence Minister Boris Pistorius that threats in outer space are being taken seriously.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he had not seen the latest news stories on the topic but that frequent reports citing “unknown sources” are “hardly worth taking seriously”.
Josef Aschbacher, head of the European Space Agency, described the presence of nuclear weapons in space as “the ultimate nightmare scenario” in comments to the Handelsblatt newspaper.
By Agence France-Presse
